subject: physics
name: Ohm's Law
vars: voltage across the conductor, in volts
summary: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, as long as its resistance and temperature stay constant.
story: Imagine a water tank on a hill. The height of the tank is the voltage V, the push that sends water down a pipe. A thin, rough pipe is the resistance R and slows the flow. The water that leaves each second is the current I. Raise the tank and more water flows. Make the pipe thinner and less flows.
analogy: Think of traffic on a road. The push from the junction is V, a narrow lane full of potholes is R, and the number of vehicles that get through each minute is I.
trick: Draw a triangle with V on top and I and R at the bottom. Cover the letter you want: V = I × R, I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I.
tip: Ohm's law applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature. On a graph of V against I, the slope equals R.

subject: physics
name: Newton's Second Law
summary: The net force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration, so the same push speeds up a lighter object more than a heavier one.
story: At a railway station, two friends give the same push to two trolleys. The empty trolley shoots ahead because its mass is small. The one stacked with luggage barely moves. The force F is the same, the mass m is different, so the acceleration a is different. To move the heavy trolley as fast, they need a bigger push.
analogy: Pushing an empty auto-rickshaw is very different from pushing a fully loaded one. With the same push, the loaded one picks up speed far more slowly.
trick: Picture the loaded trolley: for the same F, a bigger m means a smaller a. Then rearrange the formula to a = F ÷ m.
tip: F is the net (resultant) force, not just one of the forces. The unit is the newton, where 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². If the net force is zero, the acceleration is zero.

subject: physics
name: Kinetic Energy
summary: The kinetic energy of a moving object is half its mass times the square of its speed, so speed matters far more than mass.
story: A cricket ball bowled at 70 km/h is easy to block. The same ball at 140 km/h carries four times the energy, because speed is squared. Doubling the mass would only double the energy, but doubling the speed quadruples it. That is why fast bowlers are dangerous.
analogy: Think of a vehicle on a highway. At double the speed it needs about four times the braking distance, because it has four times the energy to get rid of.
trick: Say it as 'half m v v'. The speed appears twice, so it is squared.
tip: Doubling the speed makes KE four times larger, while doubling the mass only doubles it. KE is never negative. The unit is the joule.

subject: physics
name: First Equation of Motion
summary: The final velocity equals the initial velocity plus the acceleration multiplied by the time, for straight-line motion with constant acceleration.
story: A bus leaves a stop already moving at speed u. Every second the driver presses the accelerator and adds a little more speed, which is the acceleration a. After t seconds the speedometer shows v: the speed it started with plus everything it gained.
analogy: Think of a bank balance. u is the opening balance, a is the amount you save each month, t is the number of months, and v is the balance you have now.
trick: Read it as 'Final = Start + Gain', where the gain is a × t.
tip: Use it only for constant acceleration. Give a a negative sign when the object slows down, and keep the units consistent: m/s, m/s² and s.

subject: chemistry
name: Ideal Gas Law
summary: For an ideal gas, pressure times volume equals the number of moles times the gas constant times the absolute temperature.
story: Think of a sealed flask as a classroom of gas particles. More students (n) or a hotter, more excited room (T) means harder bumping into the walls, so the pressure P rises. Give them a bigger room V and the bumping eases.
analogy: Think of a bicycle tyre. Pump in more air (n) and the pressure P rises. Leave it in the hot sun (T) and it gets harder. The tyre's fixed size is V.
trick: Say the letters in order: P V n R T, or use the line 'Please Visit Nandu's Restaurant Today'.
tip: Temperature must be in kelvin (K = °C + 273). Pick the value of R to match your units: 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) or 8.314 J/(mol·K).

subject: chemistry
name: Boyle's Law
summary: At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is inversely proportional to its volume, so P times V stays constant.
story: Put your thumb over the tip of a syringe and pull the plunger. The volume grows and the push you feel from the air drops. Now press the plunger in: the volume shrinks and the pressure builds. When one goes up the other goes down, and their product stays the same.
analogy: Think of people in a lift. The smaller the lift (volume), the harder they press on each other and the walls (pressure).
trick: Picture a seesaw with P on one end and V on the other. When one rises the other falls, and P × V stays the same.
tip: It needs a constant temperature and a fixed amount of gas. The graph of P against V is a curve (a hyperbola), while P against 1/V is a straight line.

subject: chemistry
name: Molarity
formula: M = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution
summary: Molarity tells you how many moles of solute are dissolved in each litre of solution.
story: Priya makes chai for the whole family. One spoon of sugar in a cup tastes mild, and three spoons in the same cup tastes sweet. The spoons are the moles of solute, the cup is the volume, and the sweetness is the molarity.
analogy: Think of cold drink syrup. More syrup in the same glass gives a stronger drink, and the same amount of syrup in a bigger glass gives a weaker one.
trick: Moles on top, litres at the bottom. The unit itself, mol/L, gives you the formula.
tip: Use the volume of the whole solution in litres, not the volume of the solvent. Convert mL to L by dividing by 1000. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass.

subject: chemistry
name: pH
summary: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration, so a lower pH means a more acidic solution.
story: Imagine H⁺ ions as guests at a party. When the hall is packed, the host takes the negative log and reports a small number, so pH 1 means a crowded, strongly acidic party. An almost empty hall gives a large number, such as pH 13.
analogy: Think of the Richter scale for earthquakes. Each step is a tenfold change, so pH 3 has ten times more H⁺ than pH 4.
trick: The letter p stands for the power of ten. If [H⁺] = 10⁻³ mol/L, the power is −3, so pH = 3.
tip: Each pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. At 25 °C, pH 7 is neutral and pH + pOH = 14.

subject: maths
name: Quadratic
summary: It gives the roots of any quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 using only its three coefficients.
story: A ball is thrown up and a student wants to know when it lands. The height equation is quadratic. Instead of guessing, she puts a, b and c into the formula. The part under the root, b² − 4ac, is the gatekeeper: positive lets in two answers, zero lets in one, negative lets in none.
analogy: Think of a master key for quadratics. Whatever a, b and c you bring, the formula finds the roots whenever they exist.
trick: Say it like a rhyme: x equals minus b, plus or minus the square root, b squared minus four a c, all over two a.
tip: Check that a is not zero. The discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides the roots: D > 0 gives two real roots, D = 0 gives equal roots, and D < 0 gives no real roots. The sum of the roots is −b/a and the product is c/a.

subject: maths
name: Pythagoras Theorem
vars: the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle
the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle
summary: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
story: A ladder leans against a wall. The wall is one side, the ground is another, and the ladder is the longest side, the hypotenuse. A 5 m ladder with its foot 3 m from the wall reaches 4 m up the wall, because 3² + 4² = 5².
analogy: Think of crossing a rectangular park diagonally instead of walking along two edges. The shortcut is shorter, and its length comes from the formula.
trick: Memorise the triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and 8-15-17, and their multiples. Spot one in a question and skip the calculation.
tip: It works only for right-angled triangles. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always the longest side. Square each side first, then add.

subject: maths
name: Basic Trigonometric Identity
summary: For any angle θ, the square of the sine plus the square of the cosine is always equal to 1.
story: Picture a point moving around a circle of radius 1. Its height is sin θ and its horizontal distance from the centre is cos θ. Those two distances and the radius 1 form a right triangle, so Pythagoras gives sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, wherever the point stops.
analogy: Think of two friends sharing one pizza. When one takes more, the other has less, but their squared shares always make exactly one whole.
trick: Say 'sin square plus cos square is one' like a rhyme. Divide by cos²θ to get 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, and by sin²θ to get 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.
tip: It holds for every angle, so use it to swap sin²θ for 1 − cos²θ and the other way round. The square belongs to sin and cos, not to θ.

subject: maths
name: Compound Interest
vars: principal, the money you start with
rate of interest per year, in percent
summary: With compound interest, each year's interest is added to the principal, so the amount after n years is P times (1 + r/100) raised to the power n.
story: Aman deposits Rs 10,000 at 10% a year. After year one the bank adds Rs 1,000. In year two it pays interest on Rs 11,000, not Rs 10,000, so the total becomes Rs 12,100. Each year the money earns on its earlier earnings too, like a snowball growing as it rolls.
analogy: Think of a snowball rolling downhill. It picks up more snow with every turn, and the bigger it gets, the faster it grows.
trick: Say 'principal times growth factor, n times'. The growth factor is 1 plus the rate as a fraction. Then CI = A − P.
tip: For half-yearly compounding use rate r/2 and 2n periods, and for quarterly use r/4 and 4n. Compound interest is the amount minus the principal. For 2 years, CI = P × (r/100) × (2 + r/100).

subject: biology
name: Photosynthesis
vars: carbon dioxide, taken in through the stomata
glucose, the food made by the plant
summary: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, mainly in the chloroplasts of their leaves.
story: A leaf is a tiny kitchen. Sunlight is the gas flame and chlorophyll is the chef. The ingredients are six CO₂ from the air and six H₂O from the soil. The chef cooks one glucose to feed the plant, and six O₂ steam out through the stomata for us to breathe.
analogy: Think of a solar-powered kitchen. It takes sunlight, air and water, and delivers food (glucose) with oxygen as a by-product.
trick: Count it as 6, 6, 1, 6: six CO₂, six H₂O, one glucose, six O₂.
tip: The oxygen released comes from water, not from carbon dioxide. The light reactions happen in the thylakoids and the Calvin cycle in the stroma. The equation is balanced: 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side.

subject: biology
name: Cellular Respiration
vars: the energy currency of the cell
summary: Cells break down glucose with oxygen to release energy as ATP, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
story: The glucose made by the leaf is a packed lunch. In the cell's power station, the mitochondrion, the lunch is burnt with six O₂ to give the cell energy to work. The smoke that leaves is six CO₂ and six H₂O, the very ingredients photosynthesis started with.
analogy: Think of a petrol engine. Fuel (glucose) burns with oxygen, the engine gets energy, and the exhaust is carbon dioxide and water.
trick: It is photosynthesis run backwards. Learn one equation, flip it to get the other, and swap 'light energy' for 'ATP energy'.
tip: Many textbooks give about 36 to 38 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration, but counts vary, so follow your syllabus. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, while the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain are in the mitochondria.

subject: biology
name: Hardy-Weinberg
summary: In a population that is not evolving, allele frequencies p and q stay constant, and genotype frequencies follow p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
story: In a village, every gene comes in two versions, dominant p and recessive q, and marriages are random. Two dominant copies: p × p. Two recessive copies: q × q. One of each can happen in two ways: 2pq. Every villager falls in one of these groups, so together they make 1.
analogy: It is just (p + q)² expanded. Because p + q = 1, squaring both sides gives p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
trick: Remember the algebra identity (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Replace a with p and b with q.
tip: It assumes no mutation, no migration, no natural selection, random mating and a very large population. If q² is given, take the square root to find q, then p = 1 − q.

subject: biology
name: Mendel's Monohybrid Ratio
summary: When two heterozygous (Tt) parents are crossed, the F2 offspring show a 3:1 phenotypic ratio and a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio.
story: Mendel crossed tall and dwarf pea plants, and every F1 plant was tall (Tt). When those plants were crossed with each other, the dwarf trait came back like a hidden guest: one plant in four was dwarf. Three tall to one dwarf, a ratio he found again and again.
analogy: Think of tossing two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT. If H is the dominant allele, three of the four outcomes have at least one H, which gives the 3:1 ratio.
trick: Draw the Punnett square with four boxes: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Three look tall and one looks dwarf, so the phenotype is 3:1, and the genotypes read TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1.
tip: The phenotypic ratio is 3:1 but the genotypic ratio is 1:2:1, so do not mix them up. A test cross of a Tt plant with tt gives 1:1.
